title: Linking words in writing
subtitle: firstly, in other words, to sum up
summary: Organise a formal text with linking words that list points, explain and exemplify, and refer backwards and forwards in your writing.

lesson.heading: Listing your points
lesson.text: A formal text usually moves through a list of points. Start with **first**, **firstly** or **first of all**, continue with **secondly**, **thirdly** and **next**, and close the list with **finally** or **lastly**.

examples.text: **Next**, it is important to remember that ...

lesson.heading: Changing and limiting the topic
lesson.text: These phrases tell the reader what you are about to do with the topic: move to a new one, set one aside, or add a side point that is not part of the main argument.

examples.text: **Turning to** the question of foreign policy, ...
**Leaving aside** the question of pollution, there are also other reasons ...
examples.note: the writer will not deal with that question here

examples.text: **In parenthesis**, let us not forget that ...
examples.note: a side issue, not part of the main argument

lesson.heading: Summing up and finishing
rows: listing or summing up the main points
this is the end of the text
the final point on a list
lesson.note: In conclusion just means the text is ending; in summary means you are gathering up the arguments.

lesson.heading: lastly or at last?

left.label: lastly - making a final point
examples: **Lastly**, let us consider what the future holds.
**Lastly**, how can we help victims of crime?

right.label: at last - finally, after a long time
examples: **At last** I've finished my essay - what a relief!
It took three hours, but **at last** the train arrived.

lesson.note: Do not write ~~At last let us consider ...~~ when you mean Lastly.

lesson.heading: Explaining, exemplifying and rephrasing
lesson.text: Use these when you want to say the same thing differently, or to give an example. **That is to say** is much more formal than **in other words**; **as it were** is more formal than **so to speak**.

examples.text: A lot of recycling is needed; **in other words**, you have to study the same words over and over again.
Some English words are hard to pronounce, **for example**, 'eighth'.
It might be possible, **say**, to include the parents in the discussion.
examples.note: say is similar to for example; note the commas before and after

examples.text: The Parliament has different committees. **Briefly**, these consist of two main types.
examples.note: the explanation will be short and not comprehensive

examples.text: She is, **so to speak**, living in a world of her own.
examples.note: makes what you say sound less definite

lesson.heading: Referring backwards and forwards
rows: introduces a list that comes next
examples will be given later in the text
turn the page and you will find it
may I ask you to look at ... (formal)
links a letter or email to an earlier text (formal)

lesson.text: Open a formal letter or email with *With reference to your email of 12th March, ...* - it connects your message to the earlier one in one short phrase.

exercises.prompt: Match each linking phrase with its function.

pairs.right: as an aside, a secondary issue
this document is about another one
read something earlier in the text

exercises.prompt: ___, it is important to understand why people commit crimes.
exercises.explanation: Firstly, first and first of all all open a list of points.

exercises.prompt: What are the motives which make people do things they would never normally do? ___, why do they act out of character?
exercises.explanation: In other words rephrases the point you have just made.

exercises.prompt: ___, a young man steals clothes from a shop - does he do it because it is an exciting risk?
exercises.explanation: For example and for instance both introduce an illustration.

exercises.prompt: ___, it is essential to consider whether punishment makes any difference.
exercises.hint: (one word - the next point on a list)
exercises.explanation: Next moves the reader on to the following point.

exercises.prompt: Is punishment just, ___, a kind of revenge?
exercises.explanation: As it were makes what you say sound less definite; it is more formal than so to speak.

exercises.prompt: ___, how can we help victims of crime?
exercises.explanation: Lastly introduces a final point; at last means finally after a long time.

exercises.prompt: ___, how can we get to the roots of the problem, rather than just attacking the symptoms?
exercises.explanation: In summary or, more formally, in sum sums up the arguments; in conclusion would only mean the text is ending.

exercises.prompt: Which linking word is based on the verb 'to follow'?
exercises.explanation: The following points will be covered in this essay - it introduces a list.

exercises.prompt: Which word means 'turn the page and you will find it'?
exercises.explanation: A full list is given overleaf - leaf means a page of a book.

exercises.prompt: Which word is a form of the word 'far', used in 'for ___ details, see Chapter 4'?
exercises.explanation: For further details or further discussion, see Chapter 4.

exercises.prompt: Sort these phrases by what they do in a text.
categories: Refer to another part of the text

exercises.statement: At last let us consider what the future holds.
exercises.explanation: Lastly, let us consider what the future holds. At last means finally after a long time.

exercises.prompt: Put this opening of a formal letter in order.
exercises.answer: With reference to the article in your newspaper about the closure of Newton Hospital, I would like to express my strong opposition.
exercises.explanation: With reference to links your letter to an earlier text.
